Income tax: loan made by company to subsidiary - assignment by company of right to receive interest from subsidiary - whether sum received in consideration of assignment constituted 'income' - whether profit-making scheme - whether assignment fell within s.260 Income Tax Assessment Act. Income Tax Assessment Act, 1936 s.260 ; sub-secn.25(1); para 26(a) Commissioner of Taxation v. Phillips [1936] HCA 11 ; (1936) 55 C.L.R. 144 cons. Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. Paget (1938) 2 K.B. 25 cons. Shepherd v. The Commissioner of Taxation [1965] HCA 70 ; (1965) 113 C.L.R. 385 cons. W.P.Keighery Pty. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Taxation [1957] HCA 2 ; (1957) 100 C.L.R. 66 cons. Newton v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation (1958) A.C. 450 cons. Mullins v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation (1976) 135 C.L.R. 467 cons. Cridland v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1977] HCA 61 ; (1977) 140 C.L.R. 330 cons. Slutzkin v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation (1977) 140 C.L.R. 314 cons. Income Tax - Assessable income - Assignment of right to receive interest instalments - Profits of a business or realisation of a capital asset - Sale of property acquired for purposes of resale - Whether "profit" - Whether profit-making scheme - Arrangements void against Commissioner - Whether antecedent transaction - Whether ordinary business dealing - "Choice" principle - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 25(1), 26(a), 260 . Held: (1) That where a taxpayer assigned its right to receive instalments of interest falling due over the next seven years on a loan made by it a few days earlier, the sum received in consideration for the assignment was a capital receipt. So held because: (a) the consideration was not interest or equivalent to, or in substitution for, interest; (b) the transaction was not one in the ordinary course of, or an incident of, the carrying on of the taxpayer's business or course of dealing; (c) (per Fox J): the contractual right to receive the interest instalments was an asset which did not form part of the taxpayer's stock in trade. (2) No part of the consideration was a "profit" within the meaning of s 26(a) of the Income Tax Assessment Act . So held because: (a) (per Fox J): the consideration was paid as a recompense for deprivation of the interest over the period of the loan; (b) (per Lockhart J): the consideration was the present value of the taxpayer's rights to interest over the period of the loan, and there could be no element of profit in that receipt; (e) (per Jenkinson J): the cost to the taxpayer of what it sold included the contractual obligation it incurred to lend the principal moneys for seven years, and there was no evidence to suggest that the consideration exceeded the value of that obligation. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. Becker [1952] HCA 77 ; (1952) 87 CLR 456 , applied. (3) (per Fox and Lockhart JJ): There was no profit-making undertaking or scheme within the meaning of s 26(a) of the Act. (4) The assignment was not rendered void for tax purposes by s 260 of the Act because the loan agreement and the assignment did not involve a relevant alteration in the incidence of tax, there being no antecedent transaction for which the loan agreement and/or assignment could be said to have been substituted. Mullens v. Commissioner of Taxation (Cth) [1976] HCA 47 ; (1976) 135 CLR 290 ; Slutzkin v. Commissioner of Taxation (Cth) (1977) 140 CLR 314, applied. (5) (per Fox J): The transaction was outside the scope of s 260 for the further reasons that: (a) it was capable of being explained by reference to "ordinary business dealings", (b) the taxpayer entered into a scheme which made use of the choice offered by s 80 of the Act, in that the scheme was possible only because the assignee was able to offset the receipt of the assigned interest against unrecouped prior years' losses. Newton v. Commissioner of Taxation (Cth) (1958) AC 450 ; W P Keighery Pty Ltd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1957] HCA 2 ; (1957) 100 CLR 66 , applied.

Income Tax - assessable income - joint venture involving taxpayer for construction and letting of building - both companies to subscribe for one-half of shares of subsidiary - subsidiary to enter construction agreement with taxpayer and to own land - sale of shares in subsidiary - intention of taxpayer on acquisition of shares - diversification of taxpayer's business - whether sale part of business - further allotment of shares pursuant to sale agreement - whether "profit" made by taxpayer. Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 , ss. 25(1), 26(a), 26AAA Income Tax - Assessable income - Taxpayer a construction company engaged also in property development and sales - Joint venture for construction and letting of building - Taxpayer and co-venturer taking shares in operating company - Operating company holding land and contracting with taxpayer for construction of building thereon - Taxpayer selling shares in operating company - Intention of taxpayer on acquisition of shares - Whether acquisition and sale part of taxpayer's diversified business - Whether profit assessable income - Quantifying "profit" where sale of shares preceded by further allotment to taxpayer - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 25(1), 26(a), 26AAA. The taxpayer was a construction company which also engaged in other business activities including land development and the construction and sale of homes and other buildings. It accepted a proposal to become involved in the construction and letting of a commercial building on land owned by Tower Property Development Pty Ltd (TPD), an unrelated company whose shares were beneficially owned by Investment and Merchant Finance Co. Ltd (IMFC). The project was undertaken in the following manner. In February 1972 shares in TPD were allotted to the taxpayer and IMFC giving each a 50 per cent shareholding. The taxpayer entered into a construction agreement with TPD for the erection of the building. To finance part of the building costs, TPD procured a loan, repayable over twenty-five years, from an unrelated lender. There were also other financing arrangements made, the overall effect of which would have been that little in the way of dividends would flow to the taxpayer in the early years compensated by a higher dividend flow in the later years. Soon after the taxpayer acquired its shares, an offer to purchase "the project" was received from a third party but rejected. In late 1972 the taxpayer tried unsuccessfully to re-interest that party in the project. By February 1973 the taxpayer was actively seeking potential purchasers, and a buyer was found in May 1973. The taxpayer sold its shares in TPD by a contract in November 1973. Under that contract, the taxpayer was required to use part of the sale proceeds to take up further shares in TPD to enable that company to discharge its external liabilities. The balance of the sale proceeds were then paid to the taxpayer in exchange for a transfer of all its shares in TPD. The building was not completed when the sale took place. The evidence showed that the taxpayer's decision to become involved in the leasing, instead of the immediate sale, of a building to be constructed by it represented a view held by some of its directors that the taxpayer should diversify its activities, and the project provided a suitable opportunity to initiate that new policy. It was said that the project offered the taxpayer profit on the building contract, dividend income in the long term from the rental income of TPD, and an increase in the value of its shares as a result of any increased value of the property. The Commissioner, relying on s.26AAA of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth) assessed the taxpayer on a large part of its total profit from the sale of all the shares, on the grounds that it represented the profit made on the acquisition and sale, within twelve months, of the shares allotted in November 1973. In the Supreme Court of Victoria, it was held that the total profit was assessable because the taxpayer had failed to show that the profit was not income according to ordinary concepts under s. 25(1) or, alternatively, assessable income under s. 26(a). Held (dismissing the appeal): (1) The acquisition of the shares was an integral part of a wider transaction each aspect of which, as well as the transaction as a whole, had profit as the motive. It was not the mere realisation of an investment but an act done in what was truly the carrying on of a business. (2) The first transaction to give effect to the new policy of diversification cannot properly be regarded as an isolated transaction merely because it has been shown that the policy was not thereafter fully effectuated. In this regard, it is irrelevant that the taxpayer did not enter into further such transactions for a substantial period, and then only infrequently. (3) No part of the total profit resulted from the sale of the additional shares allotted in November 1973. This is because, commercially, the cost to the taxpayer included any loss in value to its initial shares in TPD, which was "transferred" from those shares when a further allotment to it was made.

Taxation - Appeal from assessment - Lump sums paid to taxpayers by company and by superannuation funds - Whether payment "in consequence of retirement from or termination of, any office or employment" - Whether payment an allowance, gratuity, benefit or bonus given by employer - Whether sums paid by company to taxpayers deductible from its assessable income. Income Tax Assessment Act, ss. 26(d) (e), 78 (l) (c). Income Tax - Assessable income - Allowable deductions - Business of company sold - Whether sums paid to former directors assessable as retiring allowances - Whether employee benefits - Whether payments deductible - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 26(d), 26(e), 51(1), 78(1)(c), 190(b). The appellant (Paklan) was a company of which the three other appellants had been directors (the directors). On 30 June 1977 Paklan ceased to carry on the business of consulting engineers. On 1 July 1977 another company with the same directors bought Paklan's business and started carrying it on at the same premises with the same employees. Some time later Paklan paid retiring sums to the directors. The directors also received payments from a directors' fund based partly on assurance policies. (1) Paklan claimed a deduction for the sums it paid. The Commissioner disallowed the claim and Paklan unsuccessfully appealed to the Supreme Court of Victoria, then further appealed. (2) The Commissioner assessed the directors on the retiring sums and other payments. They unsuccessfully appealed to the Supreme Court, then further appealed. Held (by majority): Appeals allowed in part. (1) (per the Court). The payments were not deductible by Paklan under s. 51(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act because they were paid after Paklan ceased carrying on business. (By majority) however part of the payments were deductible under s. 78(1)(c) to the extent they were made in good faith in consideration for past services. (2) (per the Court). The retiring sums paid to the directors were assessable under s. 26(e) because on the facts they were not paid in consequence of retirement (McIntosh v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation (1979) 45 CLR 279) , (by majority). However the payments from the directors' fund were on the facts capital, and not assessable under s. 26(d) or 26(e) (Constable v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation (1952) 86 CLR 403).

Income Tax - Allowable Deductions - Bad debts - Interest on loans in ordinary course of business credited to suspended interest account when debts thought doubtful and written-off when they became bad - Interest not brought to account by Bank as assessable income - Change of accountancy procedure - Whether available as source of deduction under sub-s.63(1) or sub-s.51(1) - Whether interest is "in respect of money lent". Income Tax - Assessable income - Lump sum payments made by new members to old members of Bankcard Scheme - Whether payments are income in hands of old members - Whether payments are reimbursement of expenses previously claimed as deductions. Income Tax - Allowable deductions - Bad debts - Interest on loans made in ordinary course of money lending business written off as bad debts - Interest not brought to account as assessable income - Whether deduction allowable for interest component of bad debts - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 51(1), 63 (1). Income Tax - Assessable income - Lump sum payments made by new members to existing members of Bankcard scheme - Whether payments are reimbursement of expenses previously claimed as deductions - Whether payments are assessable income in hands of existing members - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 25(1), 26(j). The respondent Bank's accounting practice in respect of interest receivable on loans to customers was to debit the customer's account at six monthly intervals with the amount of the interest due and credit the profit and loss account. Where there was doubt whether a particular loan would be recovered, the customer's account was debited with the interest but the credit was placed to an account called a "suspended interest account" and was not credited to the profit and loss account nor was it returned as assessable income of the Bank. In 1976, it was held in a New Zealand case, Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. National Bank of New Zealand (1976) 77 ATC 6001, that interest credited to suspense accounts of this kind was assessable income. The respondent Bank accepted the judgment as applicable to its operations, and thereafter returned as assessable income interest credited to the suspended interest account from 1976 onwards. In each of the four income years ended 30 June 1976 to 1979 the Bank wrote off as bad debts various outstanding loans due by customers including amounts of interest standing to the credit of the suspended interest account referable to the periods prior to 1976. The Bank sought a deduction for the whole of the amounts written off. It was held by David Hunt J. at first instance that the Bank was entitled to a deduction under s. 51(1), but not under s. 63(1) , in respect of the interest component of the debts written off as well as the principal. In so holding, his Honour accepted the Commissioner's submission concerning s. 63(1) that the interest component fell for consideration under s. 63(1)(a) and since the interest had not been returned as assessable income, no deduction under s. 63(1) was allowable in respect of it. From this decision the Commissioner appealed concerning s. 51(1) and the Bank cross-appealed concerning s. 63(1). The second question in the appeal concerned a lump sum payment received by the Bank during the 1977 year. The Bank was a founding member of the Bankcard scheme, and it incurred, together with the other founding members, certain expenses in the setting up and commencement of the scheme in 1972. It was admitted that the Bank claimed and was allowed a deduction for its proportionate share of such expenses. In 1976, five further banks were admitted to the scheme on condition that each new member pay to the existing members an entry fee. It was admitted that the amount paid to the respondent Bank bore a proportionate relationship to the amount which it had expended and previously claimed as a deduction. The Commissioner argued that, inter alia, the lump sum joining fee paid by the five new members wholly represented expenses paid on revenue account by the founding banks and claimed by them as allowable deductions and the lump sum was therefore assessable income under s. 25(1) or s. 26(j) of the Act. The primary judge found that the joining fee was fixed by reference not just to the expenses which the founding members had incurred but by reference to other factors as well. His Honour found that it was impossible to dissect the lump sum and apportion it amongst the heads to which it related, and that it was impossible to attribute to portions of the lump sum an income or non-income nature or to determine whether or not they were in the nature of reimbursement of expenses. From this decision the Commissioner appealed. Held, per curiam: (1) The deduction allowable under s. 63(1)(b) in respect of bad debts of persons carrying on a money lending business is for every component part of the bad debt written off, and covers interest as well as principal. (2) The trial judge's finding that it was not possible to say that the joining fees comprised exclusively amounts paid on revenue account and allowable as deductions was a finding of fact which has not been shown to be incorrect, and therefore a submission by the Commissioner which is put on a different factual basis could not succeed. (3) The character of the receipt of the amount of the joining fees was a capital receipt representing the price paid by the entrant banks for joining the scheme and obtaining the benefit of what it offered, in particular its assets and goodwill including the right to use the Bankcard logo. Accordingly the lump sums did not fall within s. 25(1) or s. 26(j) of the Act. Burmah Steamship Company Ltd v. Commissioner of Inland Revenue (1930) 16 TC 67 , distinguished.

Income tax - capital amount of allowance, gratuity or compensation paid in lump sum - commutation of pension entitlement paid in two sums because of uncertainty as to amount of entitlement - amount of first payment not capital amount of allowance paid in lump sum. Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 , para.26(d) Income Tax - Assessable income - Lump sum superannuation on termination of employment - Uncertainty as to amount due - Interim payment received - Second payment received on final calculation of entitlement - Whether interim payment was capital amount of any allowance etc - Whether capital amount paid in a lump sum - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), s 26(d). The taxpayer, a public servant, retired in March 1977 on grounds of invalidity and became entitled, inter alia, to a lump sum benefit from the Commonwealth superannuation scheme. Due to a restructuring of the scheme some years earlier, the precise amount of his lump sum entitlement required a complex calculation and it was not immediately ascertainable at his retirement. Section 158 of the Superannuation Act 1976 (Cth) provided that where the entitlement of a retiring employee could not be paid because the amount of the benefit had not been ascertained, the Commissioner for Superannuation could direct that an interim payment be made in an amount determined by him and that any interim payment so made should be deemed to be made in respect of that benefit. In exercise of this power, the taxpayer was paid $27,707.69 in April 1977. He received a further amount of $10,315.85 in December 1978 representing the balance of his entitlement finally calculated to be $38,023.54. The Commissioner of Taxation assessed the taxpayer under s 26(d) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 on $1,385 being 5 per cent of the amount of the interim payment, but did not seek to include any part of the second payment in the taxpayer's assessable income. The taxpayer objected against his assessment. His objection was allowed by a Board of Review. An appeal by the Commissioner to the Supreme Court of the Australian Capital Territory was dismissed, and the Commissioner then appealed to the Federal Court. Throughout the various proceedings, the Commissioner did not seek to argue that the interim payment, if not within s 26(d), was assessable in full under s 26(e). Held: per Bowen CJ and Blackburn J - (1) The phrase "lump sum" in s 26(d) refers to the manner of payment of the capital amount of the allowance, gratuity or compensation in contradistinction to payment by way of instalments or successive payments. (2) It is not permissable to read "lump sum" as including the plural with the aid of s 23(b) of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 (Cth), because s 26(d) is so specific as to exhibit a contrary intention. (3) The capital amount of the allowance to which the taxpayer was entitled on retirement was $38,023.54 and, although not immediately ascertainable, the amount was capable of being rendered certain. Because the amount was not paid in a single lump sum, no part of it was assessable under s 26(d). Per Sheppard J (dissenting) - (1) Section 26(d) is concerned with what is paid, not what is payable. The interim payment was itself an allowance, and perhaps also a gratuity, the capital amount of which was $27,707.69 actually paid in a lump sum. That he was entitled eventually to be paid more is not to the point. Reseck v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1975] HCA 38 ; (1975) 133 CLR 45 and McIntosh v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation (1979) 45 FLR 279 , referred to. Statement of Brennan J in McIntosh's case (supra) at 280-281, distinguished. (2) To hold otherwise would result in both the interim payment and the final payment falling within s 26(e) and so being assessable in full. A construction which leads to such a capricious result in this and other cases where, for one reason or another, a taxpayer's entitlement to a lump sum is not satisfied by a single payment should be avoided. This conclusion does not depend upon s 15AA of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 (Cth).

Income Tax - shares purchased with a view to making a loss - taxation avoidance scheme - whether loss deductible if sale within 12 months regardless of purpose of acquisition - interpretation of s.52 - whether s.52 has restricted meaning or states a general principle - use of proviso generally and to ascertain the scope of basic words - effect of notification under s.52 which falsely states purpose of acquisition - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cwth) ss. 26(a), 26AAA, 43, 52 . Income Tax - Allowable deductions - Purchase and sale of property at loss - Transaction within twelve months pursuant to plan to produce loss - Effect of incorrect statement in notice under s. 52 that property bought to sell at profit - Whether s. 52 deductions allowable for s. 26AAA transactions, or only s. 26(a) transactions - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss. 26(a), 26AAA, 52 . The two respondents each owned an interest in a partnership business of bookmaker. The partnership bought shares in the year of income ended 30th June, 1975, and sold them at a loss of $176,995 in the same year. These transactions were part of a plan devised by an adviser which involved the purchase of shares with borrowed funds, their sale after a declaration of dividend at an amount equivalent to the cost price reduced by the amount of the dividend, the diversion of an amount equivalent to the dividend, and the borrowing of this amount and its use, with the proceeds of the sale, to pay off the original indebtedness. This sale was to produce a loss for which a deduction would be sought. The respondents for the partnership gave the Commissioner notice for the purposes of s. 52 of the Income Tax Assessment Act , and claimed as a deduction the loss for the partnership, thereby reducing its taxable income from $178,079 to $1,084. The Commissioner disallowed their claims, and the respondents successfully appealed to the Supreme Court of Victoria. The Commissioner appealed. Held, allowing the appeals that deductions under s. 52 were available only where the profit on the property sold would have been assessable under s. 26(a). The profit of the partnership, had the shares been sold at a profit, would have been assessable only under s. 26AAA, not under s. 26(a). Per Smithers and Sheppard JJ. - A notice under s. 52 which indicated that property had been bought to sell at a profit, where that was not in fact the case, was not a sufficient notice for the purposes of s. 52.

Income Tax - Assessable income - Convertibility of non-pecuniary receipt - Retail vendor of soft drinks - Provision of holiday for vendor by manufacturer - Holiday not convertible to cash - Whether holiday related to services rendered to manufacturer - Whether value of holiday assessable income - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 , ss.25(1) and 26(e). Income Tax - Assessable income - Non-pecuniary benefit - Holiday provided by manufacturer for retailer - Not convertible into money - Whether holiday income - Whether value of holiday assessable as benefit - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss. 25 (1), 26 (e). The taxpayer and her husband in partnership sold soft drinks on a door-to-door basis. They had a written agreement with a manufacturer, which provided for the hire of a truck from the manufacturer, the purchase of soft drinks from it and various other matters. The manufacturer circularized retailers like the taxpayer, who purchased soft drinks from it, with the information that it might give holidays to them at its discretion. These holidays were described as not being transferable, and cash was not available as an alternative to them. In each of three years, the manufacturer paid for transport and accommodation for the taxpayer and her husband for a holiday in either Queensland or in the Pacific. The Commissioner assessed the taxpayer on the cost of the holidays on the basis (i) that the holidays were within the ordinary concepts of income in s. 25 (1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 and (ii) they were a benefit to the taxpayer within the meaning of s. 26 (e) of that Act. The taxpayers appealed to a Board of Review, which allowed the appeals. The Commissioner appealed to the Supreme Court of Victoria, and Jenkinson J. dismissed his appeal. The Commissioner appealed to the Federal Court. Held: Per curiam, appeal dismissed - (1) The holidays were not within the ordinary concept of income in s. 25 (1) because, on the facts, they were a benefit which could not be converted to money. (2) The taxpayers were not employees of the manufacturer, but independent contractors. None of them was an "employee", and did not "render services" within the meaning of s. 26 (e). The value of the holiday fell outside the section.

Appeal - Whether decision involved a question of law - Role of appellate court. Income Tax - Assessable income - Whether shares acquired for purpose of profit-making by sale. Income Tax Assessment Act, 1936 - s.26(a), s.190(b), s.196(1). Income Tax - Appeal from decision of Board of Review - Whether question of law was involved - Appeal court's role in interfering in findings of fact - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss. 26(a), 190 (b), 196. The taxpayer was assessed under s. 26(a) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 on the profit made from the sale of some shares. The taxpayer objected, and the Commissioner disallowed the objection. The taxpayer appealed to a Board of Review, which upheld the Commissioner's decision. The taxpayer appealed to the Supreme Court of New South Wales, which allowed the appeal. The Commissioner then appealed to the Federal Court on two grounds: (1) the appeal to the Supreme Court had been incompetent because the decision of the Board of Review involved no question of law; (2) the decision of the Supreme Court was wrong on the facts. Held: Appeal dismissed - (1) Decisions in s. 26(a) cases do not necessarily involve a question of law. Lombardo v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1979] FCA 66 ; (1979), 40 FLR 208 , referred to. But the Board's decision in this case did involve a question of law, namely the onus of proof under s. 190(b). (2) There was nothing in the evidence which warranted interfering on appeal with the Supreme Court's decision on the facts. Powell v. Streatham Manor Nursing Home, (1935) AC 243 , referred to.

Income Tax - Whether land can be acquired partly for profitmaking by sale and partly as investment - Powers of court on appeal - Burden of proof on taxpayer with reference to assessment - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth.), ss. 25, 26 (a), 190 (b) - Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth.), s. 28(1)(a). The taxpayers, whose business was the purchase and subdivision of land, acquired twenty-five acres of land in 1959. On ten acres of the land were three warehouses, the other fifteen acres was vacant land. The taxpayer contended that it purchased the section of ten acres as a source of rental income and for possible subdivision and sale in the future, and the section of fifteen acres with the intention of subdivision and sale. The taxpayer from the inception let the warehouses, and returned a profit in each of the years 1960-1974. The taxpayer was forced by its creditors to commence to subdivide and sell the ten acres in 1966. The Supreme Court held that, whilst there were some features pointing to the dominant purpose of the acquisition of the ten acres being the letting of the warehouses, there were others pointing to the purpose being for subdivision and resale, and that it was acquired for resale at a profit. Held: (1) An appeal to the Federal Court of Australia is a full appeal both as to law and fact. Edwards v. Noble [1971] HCA 54 ; (1971), 125 CLR 296 , and Imperial Chemical Industries of Australia and New Zealand Ltd. v. Murphy (1973), 47 ALJR 122 , followed. (2) The finding that the dominant purpose of acquisition was resale was an inference reached by a consideration of the actual facts proved and the probabilities to which they gave rise, and because it was a matter of inference, the Federal Court was free to look at the matter for itself, not upsetting any finding of fact, unless satisfied that it was wrong. Paterson v. Paterson [1953] HCA 74 ; (1953), 89 CLR 212 ; Benmax v. Austin Motor Co. Ltd., (1955) AC 370 ; Jones v. Capaldi [1956] HCA 37 ; (1956), 98 CLR 615 , and Flannery v. Cohuna Sewerage Authority (1976), 51 ALJR 135 , referred to. (3) There is no reason in principle why, with reference to s. 26(a) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 , land may not be acquired for one purpose as to part and for another purpose as to the remainder. Chapman v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1968] HCA 4 ; (1968), 117 CLR 167 ; Smith v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation (1972), 46 ALJR 518 , referred to. (4) The dominant purpose of the acquisition of the ten acres was not that of profit-making by sale within the meaning of s. 26(a) of the Act, nor was the profit derived from the sale of the ten acres income within the ordinary concepts and so assessable under s. 25(1) of the Act. (5) The effect of s. 190(b) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 is that unless the appellant shows by evidence that the assessment is incorrect, it will prevail. McCormack v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1979] HCA 18 ; (1979), 53 ALJR 436 , followed.

Courts - Federal Court - Jurisdiction - Question reserved for consideration - Whether questions concerning matter with respect to which appeal would lie - Matter in which appeal would lie only with leave - Leave to appeal not granted - No matter with respect to which appeal would lie - No jurisdiction to consider question - Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth.), s. 26 (1). Courts - Federal Court - Practice and procedure - Special case reserving questions for consideration - Based on disputed and incomplete evidence - Not based on factual situation - Whether must be based on facts found or agreed - Mere advisory opinion - Question not considered - Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth.), s. 26 (1) - Federal Court of Australia Rules, O. 6. Income Tax - Appeals - Appeal from board of review to Supreme Court - Question of law reserved by Supreme Court for consideration by Federal Court - Circumstances in which Federal Court can or will consider question reserved - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth.), s. 196 - Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth.), s. 26 (1). A decision of the Commissioner of Taxation disallowing a claim for deductions by the taxpayer was referred to the board of review under s. 188 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (as amended). The board confirmed the assessment and the taxpayer appealed under s. 196 to the Supreme Court of South Australia. The appeal raised a question as to the construction of the repealed s. 82j (6) of the Act. The Supreme Court reserved the question of construction for consideration by the Federal Court pursuant to s. 26 of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 which provides by sub-s. (1) that: "A court from which appeals lie to the Court may state any case or reserve any question concerning a matter with respect to which such an appeal would lie from a judgment of the first-mentioned court for the consideration of the Court and the Court has jurisdiction to hear and determine the case or question." Held: The Federal Court should not answer the question referred to it and the matter should be remitted to the Supreme Court because: (1) Per Brennan and Deane JJ., Bowen C.J. not deciding - The Supreme Court had no jurisdiction to refer the question to the Federal Court and the Federal Court had no jurisdiction to answer it, either under the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 or under the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 . Section 26 of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 conferred no jurisdiction in the circumstances because: (a) pursuant to s. 196 (5) of the Income Tax Assessment Act leave would have to be granted by the Federal Court before there could be an appeal to the Federal Court against any decision of the Supreme Court; (b) leave to appeal had not been granted by the Federal Court; (c) in the absence of leave to appeal, it could not be said that the question concerned "a matter with respect to which . . . an appeal would lie" in accordance with the requirements of s. 26 (1). (2) Per curiam - Having regard to the form in which the question was reserved for consideration, it should not be considered. The question was reserved without reference to any factual context, no findings of fact having been made by the Supreme Court and no statement of facts having been agreed upon between the parties. Hence any answer of the Federal Court would constitute a mere "advisory opinion", the effectiveness of which would depend on facts yet to be determined. Whether the provisions of s. 198 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 are exhaustive of the circumstances in which a judge of a Supreme Court hearing an appeal under that Act has power to state a case for the opinion of the Federal Court so as to exclude the operation of s. 26 of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 , referred to by Deane J.

Special leave to appeal was granted in this matter in order to test the existence of a principle of law for which the appellant contended. In the notice of appeal to this Court it was expressed as a "general principle of law that an amount paid as compensation for or reimbursement of a deductible expense is income within ordinary concepts". Before the Full Court of the Federal Court [1] , on appeal from the Administrative Appeals Tribunal, and before this Court the appellant argued for such a principle while submitting that, in any event, in the circumstances of the case the amount received by the respondent was income according to ordinary concepts, hence assessable under s 25(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth) ("the Act"). He further submitted that the amount was received by the respondent as compensation for, or by way of reimbursement of, a deductible expense incurred in protecting his employment, hence assessable under s 26(e) of the Act. The claim based on s 26(e) is not before this Court. The formulation of the general principle for which the appellant contended underwent some change as the argument progressed. This was, no doubt, because of the difficulty he had in maintaining such a principle in an absolute form. And so the appellant moved in his written submissions to a substantially qualified position, expressed in the following terms: "[I]n the absence of unusual circumstances, such as:- (a) a particular provision of the Income Tax Assessment Act dealing specifically with payments of the nature in question; or (b) an intention to provide family benevolence; the true position is that:- (c) a payment made to reimburse or compensate for a deductible expense will ordinarily take its character from the nature of the expense for which it is reimbursement or compensation; (d) such a payment will ordinarily be of an income nature: there will be no feature of it to give it any other character; and (e) prima facie, the fact that it is such a reimbursement or compensation will make it income." Income Tax - Division 7 tax - Dividends - Resolution to pay interim dividend to holding company - Book entries - Resolution to rescind interim dividend - Reversal of book entries - Whether dividend "paid" or "credited" - Whether assessable - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth.), Divn 7, ss. 6 (1) definition of "paid", 44 (1) (a). Brookton appealed against a decision of Helsham C.J. in Eq. of the Supreme Court of New South Wales that it was not a co-operative company for the purposes of s. 117 (1) (d) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 , and therefore not entitled to be assessed under Divn 9 as a co-operative and under Divn 7 as a public company. Brookton's members were a group of professional men. Over three years, Brookton purchased relatively small amounts of wine for its members, and distributed rebates on wines purchased by them. At the same time, its subsidiaries engaged on a large scale in "dividend stripping" activities. The success of these operations depended on Brookton's public company status. Some of the profit of the subsidiaries' operations were distributed to Brookton's members. In one year, one of Brookton's subsidiaries declared an interim dividend to it . The dividend was expressed not to be payable until Brookton demanded it. The dividend was not demanded or paid, and the declaration of dividend was subsequently rescinded. The Commissioner assessed Brookton on the dividend. Held: (1) Brookton was not a public company for the purposes of s. 117 (1), the relevant test of which was the dominant purpose for establishing the company. On the evidence, this was not wine-buying for members, it was to hold shares in the subsidiaries, and thereby confer subsidiary status on them. (2) Per Brennan and Deane JJ., Fisher J. dissenting - On the facts, the interim dividend was not paid, so it should not have been included in the assessable income of Brookton.

Income Tax - shares purchased with a view to making a loss - taxation avoidance scheme - whether loss deductible if sale within 12 months regardless of purpose of acquisition - interpretation of s.52 - whether s.52 has restricted meaning or states a general principle - use of proviso generally and to ascertain the scope of basic words - effect of notification under s.52 which falsely states purpose of acquisition - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cwth) ss. 26(a), 26AAA, 43, 52 . Income Tax - Allowable deductions - Purchase and sale of property at loss - Transaction within twelve months pursuant to plan to produce loss - Effect of incorrect statement in notice under s. 52 that property bought to sell at profit - Whether s. 52 deductions allowable for s. 26AAA transactions, or only s. 26(a) transactions - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss. 26(a), 26AAA, 52 . The two respondents each owned an interest in a partnership business of bookmaker. The partnership bought shares in the year of income ended 30th June, 1975, and sold them at a loss of $176,995 in the same year. These transactions were part of a plan devised by an adviser which involved the purchase of shares with borrowed funds, their sale after a declaration of dividend at an amount equivalent to the cost price reduced by the amount of the dividend, the diversion of an amount equivalent to the dividend, and the borrowing of this amount and its use, with the proceeds of the sale, to pay off the original indebtedness. This sale was to produce a loss for which a deduction would be sought. The respondents for the partnership gave the Commissioner notice for the purposes of s. 52 of the Income Tax Assessment Act , and claimed as a deduction the loss for the partnership, thereby reducing its taxable income from $178,079 to $1,084. The Commissioner disallowed their claims, and the respondents successfully appealed to the Supreme Court of Victoria. The Commissioner appealed. Held, allowing the appeals that deductions under s. 52 were available only where the profit on the property sold would have been assessable under s. 26(a). The profit of the partnership, had the shares been sold at a profit, would have been assessable only under s. 26AAA, not under s. 26(a). Per Smithers and Sheppard JJ. - A notice under s. 52 which indicated that property had been bought to sell at a profit, where that was not in fact the case, was not a sufficient notice for the purposes of s. 52.

A decision of the Commissioner of Taxation disallowing a claim for deductions by the taxpayer was referred to the board of review under s. 188 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (as amended). The board confirmed the assessment and the taxpayer appealed under s. 196 to the Supreme Court of South Australia. The appeal raised a question as to the construction of the repealed s. 82j (6) of the Act. The Supreme Court reserved the question of construction for consideration by the Federal Court pursuant to s. 26 of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 which provides by sub-s. (1) that: "A court from which appeals lie to the Court may state any case or reserve any question concerning a matter with respect to which such an appeal would lie from a judgment of the first-mentioned court for the consideration of the Court and the Court has jurisdiction to hear and determine the case or question." Held: The Federal Court should not answer the question referred to it and the matter should be remitted to the Supreme Court because: (1) Per Brennan and Deane JJ., Bowen C.J. not deciding - The Supreme Court had no jurisdiction to refer the question to the Federal Court and the Federal Court had no jurisdiction to answer it, either under the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 or under the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 . Section 26 of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 conferred no jurisdiction in the circumstances because: (a) pursuant to s. 196 (5) of the Income Tax Assessment Act leave would have to be granted by the Federal Court before there could be an appeal to the Federal Court against any decision of the Supreme Court; (b) leave to appeal had not been granted by the Federal Court; (c) in the absence of leave to appeal, it could not be said that the question concerned "a matter with respect to which . . . an appeal would lie" in accordance with the requirements of s. 26 (1). (2) Per curiam - Having regard to the form in which the question was reserved for consideration, it should not be considered. The question was reserved without reference to any factual context, no findings of fact having been made by the Supreme Court and no statement of facts having been agreed upon between the parties. Hence any answer of the Federal Court would constitute a mere "advisory opinion", the effectiveness of which would depend on facts yet to be determined. Whether the provisions of s. 198 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 are exhaustive of the circumstances in which a judge of a Supreme Court hearing an appeal under that Act has power to state a case for the opinion of the Federal Court so as to exclude the operation of s. 26 of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 , referred to by Deane J.

Allders International Pty Ltd v Commissioner of State Revenue in his capacity as Comptroller of Stamps Commonwealth Constitution - Exclusive legislative power - With respect to a Commonwealth place - Characterisation of State law - Whether State stamp duty payable on a lease of part of a Commonwealth place. Taxation - State stamp duty - Nature of stamp duty - Whether payable on a lease of part of a Commonwealth place. BRENNAN CJ. Tullamarine Airport was constructed on land acquired for the purpose by the Commonwealth of Australia. The Commonwealth remains registered as the proprietor of an estate in fee simple in that land. The Federal Airports Corporation Act 1986 (Cth) ("the FAC Act ") established the Federal Airports Corporation ("FAC") as a body corporate in which, pursuant to s 28(1) of that Act, Tullamarine Airport [1] was vested "without any conveyance, transfer or assignment". The FAC holds Tullamarine Airport "for and on behalf of the Commonwealth" [2] . It is a "place acquired by the Commonwealth" for a public purpose within the meaning of those words in s 52(i) of the Constitution . In exercise of its statutory powers [3] , the FAC granted a lease to the appellant ("Allders") of a shop at the Tullamarine Airport to conduct the business of a duty free and sales tax free concession. The instrument of lease demised the premises for a term certain expiring on 31 October 2000 [4] . The rent reserved was a fixed sum of $12 per annum (if demanded) plus a variable component calculated according to formulae the factors of which included the number of inbound and outbound international passengers and the average levels of their expenditure on goods to be sold by the lessee [5] . The instrument of lease was executed in New South Wales. Pursuant to s 32 of the Stamps Act 1958 (Vic) ("the Act"), Allders required the Commissioner of State Revenue in his capacity as Comptroller of Stamps of Victoria to express an opinion as to whether the instrument of lease was chargeable with duty and, if so, with what amount. In order to obtain that opinion, the solicitors for Allders lodged the executed lease with the Commissioner. The Commissioner expressed the opinion that the instrument of lease was dutiable and that duty should be assessed ad valorem on the rent calculated and paid in accordance with s 83A of the Act. Section 83A applies to a lease for a definite term of not less than 12 months where the rent cannot be ascertained at the time of execution of the lease. The calculation is based on an estimate and is re-calculated on annual re-estimates of the rent during the term of the lease. The taxpayers were husband and wife. They had carried on a rural business in equal partnership. On 18th April, 1975, Rowe Holdings Pty. Ltd. was incorporated to act as trustee of a family trust which was established on 23rd April, 1975. On 16th May, 1975, both taxpayers assigned to the company "as at and from" 1st July, 1974, one-half of their respective shares in the partnership. By deed it was provided that the taxpayers and the company would continue the partnership business. The Commissioner assessed each of the taxpayers on half of the income of the partnership for the whole of the year of income ending 30th June, 1975. The taxpayers appealed unsuccessfully to a Board of Review, and then to the Supreme Court of Queensland. The taxpayers appealed. Held, appeals allowed, that on its construction, the assignment of 16th May, 1975, terminated the existing partnership between the taxpayers and created a new partnership between the taxpayers and the company. The taxpayers were therefore each assessable on half the partnership income only up to that date. They were assessable to that date because the assignment could not operate retrospectively. Rose v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1951] HCA 68 ; (1951), 84 CLR 118 ; Commissioner of Taxation v. Happ, (1952) ALR 382 , referred to. The taxpayers and the company were assessable on their respective shares in the new partnership from that date. The assessment on the taxpayers should accordingly be set aside so that new assessments could issue.

Income Tax - Assessable income - Lump sum payments made by new members to existing members of Bankcard scheme - Whether payments are reimbursement of expenses previously claimed as deductions - Whether payments are assessable income in hands of existing members - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 25(1), 26(j). The respondent Bank's accounting practice in respect of interest receivable on loans to customers was to debit the customer's account at six monthly intervals with the amount of the interest due and credit the profit and loss account. Where there was doubt whether a particular loan would be recovered, the customer's account was debited with the interest but the credit was placed to an account called a "suspended interest account" and was not credited to the profit and loss account nor was it returned as assessable income of the Bank. In 1976, it was held in a New Zealand case, Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. National Bank of New Zealand (1976) 77 ATC 6001, that interest credited to suspense accounts of this kind was assessable income. The respondent Bank accepted the judgment as applicable to its operations, and thereafter returned as assessable income interest credited to the suspended interest account from 1976 onwards. In each of the four income years ended 30 June 1976 to 1979 the Bank wrote off as bad debts various outstanding loans due by customers including amounts of interest standing to the credit of the suspended interest account referable to the periods prior to 1976. The Bank sought a deduction for the whole of the amounts written off. It was held by David Hunt J. at first instance that the Bank was entitled to a deduction under s. 51(1), but not under s. 63(1) , in respect of the interest component of the debts written off as well as the principal. In so holding, his Honour accepted the Commissioner's submission concerning s. 63(1) that the interest component fell for consideration under s. 63(1)(a) and since the interest had not been returned as assessable income, no deduction under s. 63(1) was allowable in respect of it. From this decision the Commissioner appealed concerning s. 51(1) and the Bank cross-appealed concerning s. 63(1). The second question in the appeal concerned a lump sum payment received by the Bank during the 1977 year. The Bank was a founding member of the Bankcard scheme, and it incurred, together with the other founding members, certain expenses in the setting up and commencement of the scheme in 1972. It was admitted that the Bank claimed and was allowed a deduction for its proportionate share of such expenses. In 1976, five further banks were admitted to the scheme on condition that each new member pay to the existing members an entry fee. It was admitted that the amount paid to the respondent Bank bore a proportionate relationship to the amount which it had expended and previously claimed as a deduction. The Commissioner argued that, inter alia, the lump sum joining fee paid by the five new members wholly represented expenses paid on revenue account by the founding banks and claimed by them as allowable deductions and the lump sum was therefore assessable income under s. 25(1) or s. 26(j) of the Act. The primary judge found that the joining fee was fixed by reference not just to the expenses which the founding members had incurred but by reference to other factors as well. His Honour found that it was impossible to dissect the lump sum and apportion it amongst the heads to which it related, and that it was impossible to attribute to portions of the lump sum an income or non-income nature or to determine whether or not they were in the nature of reimbursement of expenses. From this decision the Commissioner appealed. Held, per curiam: (1) The deduction allowable under s. 63(1)(b) in respect of bad debts of persons carrying on a money lending business is for every component part of the bad debt written off, and covers interest as well as principal. (2) The trial judge's finding that it was not possible to say that the joining fees comprised exclusively amounts paid on revenue account and allowable as deductions was a finding of fact which has not been shown to be incorrect, and therefore a submission by the Commissioner which is put on a different factual basis could not succeed. (3) The character of the receipt of the amount of the joining fees was a capital receipt representing the price paid by the entrant banks for joining the scheme and obtaining the benefit of what it offered, in particular its assets and goodwill including the right to use the Bankcard logo. Accordingly the lump sums did not fall within s. 25(1) or s. 26(j) of the Act. Burmah Steamship Company Ltd v. Commissioner of Inland Revenue (1930) 16 TC 67 , distinguished.

Income Tax - Bad debts - Allowable deductions - Scheme of arrangement - Whether scheme effected change in beneficial ownership of debts - Whether at time of writing off debts, they were debts owed to taxpayer - Companies Act, 1962-1966 (S.A.), s. 181 (2) - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth.), ss. 63 (1), 80. Companies - Scheme of arrangement - Change of beneficial ownership of book debts - Companies Act, 1962-1966 (S.A.), s. 181 (2). The question before the court on appeal was whether amounts claimed were, when they were written off as bad debts, debts owed to the taxpayer. The taxpayer, a building company, entered into a scheme of arrangement which provided for a moratorium on the payment of its debts but did not involve the composition of any of the claims. The taxpayer had debts owing to it by four companies ("the development companies") which were associated with it. Those companies had substantial losses and there was no prospect of the debts being recovered. After certain intervening events, including a new scheme of arrangement, the debts the subject of the appeal were written off by the taxpayer. On 30th June, 1967, an agreement was entered into for the sale of all of the shares but one in the taxpayer, it being a term of the agreement that the purchaser would pay an amount to the taxpayer calculated by reference to the taxpayer's losses and the amount so received would be available for the taxpayer's creditors. The agreement was conditional upon creditors accepting the amount and proceeds of the realization of the taxpayer's assets in satisfaction of their claims. On 13th May, 1968, the previous scheme was terminated and a new scheme was approved by the Supreme Court of South Australia. A committee of management was appointed and it was agreed that the purchaser would lend an amount calculated by reference to the taxpayer's losses, to the committee to be held on behalf of the taxpayer and to be distributed to its creditors pro rata in full satisfaction and discharge of their claims. If the taxpayer was entitled to a deduction for the debts written off pursuant to s. 63 (1) of the Act, then the consequential losses would be of benefit to the purchaser as deductions under s. 80 (2) upon the purchaser recommencing the business. It was submitted by the commissioner that prior to the debts being written off, the beneficial ownership in the debts was assigned by the taxpayer to the committee of management to be held by them on trust for the scheme creditors. It was accepted that there has been no legal assignment of the debt. Held: (1) On a proper construction of the scheme, there was not an assignment of the debts and therefore the taxpayer was entitled to claim a deduction under s. 63 (1) of the Act. A.G.C. (Advances) Ltd. v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1975] HCA 7 ; (1975), 132 CLR 175 , followed. (2) It is necessary to look to the instrument and surrounding circumstances to ascertain the existence of an intention to assign. Smith v. Perpetual Trustee Co. Ltd. [1910] HCA 39 ; (1910), 11 CLR 148 , and Morgan v. Lariviere (1875), LR 7 HL 423 , referred to. (3) No particular form of words is necessary to effect an assignment. G. E. Crane Sales Pty. Ltd. v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1971] HCA 75 ; (1971), 126 CLR 177 , and A.G.C. (Advances) Ltd. v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1975] HCA 7 ; (1975), 132 CLR 175 , referred to. (4) The word "moneys" in the expression "any other moneys to which the company was entitled on 30th June, 1967", could include debts, particularly debts which, as here, had fallen due and were immediately repayable. Perrin v. Morgan, (1943) AC 399, referred to. In the present context "moneys" only related to money paid to the committee of management that is the money which the taxpayer had on hand. The trade debts as distinct from their proceeds fell outside cl. 9 of the scheme of arrangement. (5) The debts were not the proceeds of the realization of the taxpayer's assets, but were the assets themselves. The proceeds were the moneys received when the debts were discharged. (6) A distinction may be drawn between an obligation to pay to another the proceeds of a debt when received and an equitable assignment to another of the debt before the proceeds are received. Palette Shoes Pty. Ltd. v. Krohn (1937), 58 CLR 1 , followed. Palmer v. Culverwell, Brooks & Co. (1901), 85 LT 758 ; Norman v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1963] HCA 21 ; (1963), 109 CLR 9 , and Shepherd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1965] HCA 70 ; (1965), 113 CLR 385 , referred to.

Income Tax - Assessable income - Taxpayer severing its connection as member with company - Taxpayer receiving its share of available funds - Whether assessable as dividend - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 44 , 47 . The taxpayer received a sum as a member of a company limited by guarantee (Ogg Holdings Ltd). Part of the sum represented part of a gift made to Ogg Holdings by a Mr Ogg, then one of its shareholders. Mr Ogg was the father of Mrs Slater, whose family company the taxpayer was. Another part of the sum represented part of the capital profits made by Ogg Holdings on the sale of a shopping centre. The sum was paid to the taxpayer in consequence of its retirement from membership of Ogg Holdings. The Commissioner assessed the taxpayer on both the above parts of the sum received as dividends within s. 44(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 . The taxpayer unsuccessfully appealed to the Supreme Court of New South Wales. The taxpayer appealed. Held, (by majority, Lockhart and Fitzgerald JJ.), appeal allowed. The taxpayer had severed its connection with Ogg Holdings and what it received was its share of the available assets. This was capital in its hands, and not assessable as a dividend. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. Blakely (1951) 82 CLR 389 ; Uther v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1964] HCA 80 ; (1964) 111 CLR 318.

Bankruptcy: deeds of arrangement - whether deeds comply with the provisions of Part X of the Act - distribution clause in each deed purported to require the trustee to intermingle funds which were required by the Act to be administered separately - whether the court should declare each deed to be void or whether it should declare provisions of each deed to be void - conduct of registered trustee examined - circumstances in which a registered trustee should not accept appointment as controlling trustee or as trustee of a deed. Bankruptcy Act 1966 (C'th): SS108 ; 190 ; 222 (1), (2), (3); 237(2) Bankruptcy Rules Rule 100, Form 43 Bankruptcy - Deeds of arrangement - Whether the deeds comply with Pt X of Act - Distribution clause required trustee to intermingle funds - The Act requires these funds to be administered separately - Whether each deed to be declared void or whether distribution clause to be severed. Bankruptcy - Registered trustee - Conduct examined - Conflict of interest - Circumstances barring a registered trustee from accepting appointment as controlling trustee or trustee of a deed - Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth), ss 108 , 109 , 222 (1), (2), (3), 237(2) - Bankruptcy Rules, r. 100. In 1977 a group of medical practitioners, including each of the twelve debtors named as respondent to these applications before the Federal Court of Australia, embarked upon the business venture of establishing a private hospital. When they ran into financial difficulties meetings of creditors were held. In the case of each debtor an almost identical deed of arrangement was agreed to and executed by each debtor on 25 May 1981. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxation applied in each case for the deed to be declared void and to be terminated. At the wish of all parties all the applications were heard together. The full facts of the case including the text of cl. 3 of the deed of arrangement in the judgment is set out. Held, that in each of these cases the deed of arrangement is declared void on the ground that it does not comply with the requirements of Pt X of the Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) (the Act). Nor does it comply substantially, within the meaning of that phrase in s. 222(3) of the Act, with those requirements because: (1) In order to comply with Pt X of the Act, a deed of arrangement of an individual debtor must require the trustee to hold his contributions upon trust for his creditors, to be distributed rateably among them. Attorney-General of Ontario v. Attorney-General for the Dominion of Canada (1894) AC 189 , referred to. (2) The resolution proposed and accepted by each meeting of creditors was fundamentally based on the creditors receiving the fruits of the distribution prescribed by cl. 3 and granting in return the right to the release and discharge provided by cl. 4. (3) To use the power of severance so as to strike out the substance of cl. 3 would be to produce in each case a fundamentally different deed from that for which the creditors voted. Duties of a registered trustee considered.

Bankruptcy - property recovered or preserved by means of an indemnity for costs of litigation given by creditors other than the Deputy Commissioner of Taxation - Whether the power of the Court under s.109(6) of the Bankruptcy Act 1966 to make an order with respect to the distribution of the proceeds of that property with a view to giving the indemnifying creditors an advantage over other creditors is subject to ss. 221P and 221YU of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 . Bankruptcy - Litigation of bankrupt continued by virtue of indemnity - Indemnity provided by certain creditors only - Litigation successful - Deputy Commissioner of Taxation not indemnifying creditor - Claim of Deputy Commissioner to priority - Whether discretion of court subject to statutory priority - Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth), s. 109 (1), (6) - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss. 221P, 221YU. The official receiver was trustee of the property of the bankrupt. Early in the course of the bankruptcy six creditors, not including the Deputy Commissioner of Taxation, provided the official receiver with indemnities in respect of the costs of certain litigation already commenced on behalf of the bankrupt prior to the bankruptcy, without which it would not have been possible to continue the litigation. Subsequently the action was settled and after the deduction of certain costs and expenses the sum of $1,732.80 remained available for distribution to creditors. By application dated 14th August, 1980, the official receiver sought directions and orders pursuant to s. 109 (6) of the Bankruptcy Act 1966 as to the manner of applying the proceeds recovered by means of the indemnity for costs. The Deputy Commissioner gave notice that he intended to oppose the making of the orders sought on the grounds that he had a statutory priority pursuant to s. 221P (2) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 which could not be displaced by order of the court. Further by application on 22nd October, 1980, the Deputy Commissioner sought orders in relation to the net proceeds resulting from the litigation; the official receiver gave notice of opposition to the orders sought by the Deputy Commissioner. Held, that the statutory priority granted to the Deputy Commissioner of Taxation pursuant to s. 109 (1) of the Bankruptcy Act applies only to the distribution of proceeds pursuant to that section. It does not affect any distribution made pursuant to an order of the court under s. 109 (6) of the Act. In the present circumstances, having regard to the facts of the case, it was appropriate to give the indemnifying creditors the advantage over other creditors of having the whole of the sum recovered by means of their indemnity distributed amongst them in proportion to the amounts of their respective debts. Orders accordingly.

Income Tax Assessment Act, 1936-1975: ss. 90, 91, 92 Income Tax - Assessable income - Partnership - Assignment of share in partnership to company - Assignment expressed to operate retrospectively - Whether assignment terminated existing partnership - Whether original partners assessable on partnership income up to assignment date - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss. 90 , 91 , 92 . The taxpayers were husband and wife. They had carried on a rural business in equal partnership. On 18th April, 1975, Rowe Holdings Pty. Ltd. was incorporated to act as trustee of a family trust which was established on 23rd April, 1975. On 16th May, 1975, both taxpayers assigned to the company "as at and from" 1st July, 1974, one-half of their respective shares in the partnership. By deed it was provided that the taxpayers and the company would continue the partnership business. The Commissioner assessed each of the taxpayers on half of the income of the partnership for the whole of the year of income ending 30th June, 1975. The taxpayers appealed unsuccessfully to a Board of Review, and then to the Supreme Court of Queensland. The taxpayers appealed. Held, appeals allowed, that on its construction, the assignment of 16th May, 1975, terminated the existing partnership between the taxpayers and created a new partnership between the taxpayers and the company. The taxpayers were therefore each assessable on half the partnership income only up to that date. They were assessable to that date because the assignment could not operate retrospectively. Rose v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1951] HCA 68 ; (1951), 84 CLR 118 ; Commissioner of Taxation v. Happ, (1952) ALR 382 , referred to. The taxpayers and the company were assessable on their respective shares in the new partnership from that date. The assessment on the taxpayers should accordingly be set aside so that new assessments could issue.

Income Tax - Leases - Expenditure on dredging leased seabed - Dredged soil used to build up adjacent land - Deduction for expenditure by lessee - All expenditure reimbursed by port authority on surrender of leases - "Recoupment" - Whether seabed used to produce assessable income - Whether dredging constitutes "improvement" - Whether land subject to tenant rights - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth.), ss. 85, 87, 88, 122, 122A, 122E, 122T, 123, 123A, 123B. The taxpayer was one of a group of five companies carrying on mining operations in Western Australia. They used Port Hedland as a point of despatch for ore mined by it. The five companies held three leases of land in the vicinity of the port. Two of them, the inner harbour and the outer channel leases, were leases of areas of seabed. The third ("the industrial lease") was of low lying land adjacent to the harbour. The leases required the taxpayer to deepen the harbour. This was done by dredging. The dredged soil was taken ashore and used to build up the land comprising the railway lease. Dredging was the cheapest way of providing soil to build up the railway lease. Building up the railway lease was the cheapest method of disposing of the dredged soil. The harbour leases contained provisions requiring surrender of the leases to a port authority if requested by the relevant Minister. In the event of surrender, the taxpayer was entitled to be reimbursed all dredging costs, including amounts paid to Goldsworthy Mining Ltd. which had performed some of the dredging for the taxpayer. The leases were duly surrendered upon the requirement of the Minister, and the taxpayer became entitled to receive compensation accordingly. Compensation was by forty quarterly payments, with provision for deferment. Any deferment, however, did not operate to reduce the total amount of compensation ultimately paid. The Commissioner treated the cost of the dredging and filling operation as being attributable as to twenty-seven per cent to dredging and transporting the soil, and as to seventy-three per cent to the remainder of the work. In addition to dredging, the taxpayer had installed navigation aids in the harbour - some fixed to the leased seabed, some attached by cables to weights resting on the leased seabed. The taxpayer claimed deductions under Pt III Divn 10 AAA for the capital costs associated with dredging the seabed and spreading the soil on land to be used for a railway. The Commissioner allowed the deduction as to seventy-three per cent. For the Commissioner it was submitted that none of the expenditure was expenditure in relation to earthworks (s. 123 (2)), that it was wholly expenditure in respect of port facilities (s. 123 (2)) and that by virtue of the right to compensation which accrued on surrender of the leases, the expenditure was deemed not to be deductible, by reason of s. 123A (2). The taxpayer also sought the deductions under Pt III Divn 10. The Commissioner allowed the deductions as to seventy-three per cent, but argued that none of the expenditure was deductible by reason of the right of compensation and the provisions of s. 122T. In relation to the claims under Divn 10A and 10AAA the Commissioner submitted in the alternative that the twenty-seven/seventy-three apportionment of the total cost of the dredging and filling operation was not unreasonable. The taxpayer argued that the expenditure was deductible under s. 88 (2) as improvements not subject to tenant rights. The taxpayer also argued that the expenditure was deductible under s. 85 as amounts paid by a lessee in effecting improvements where the lease is surrendered during the year of income. Held: dismissing the taxpayer's appeals and allowing the Commissioner's appeals: (1) The right to compensation for capital expenditure which accrued on the surrender of the leases was a recoupment for the purposes of s. 123A (2) and the expenditure was therefore deemed never to have been deductible. (2) By parity of reasoning there had been a recoupment for the purposes of s. 122T. (3) For the purposes of the claim under s. 88, the proportion of total expenditure attributed by the Commissioner to improvements of the industrial lease was adequate. (4) The seabed was not land used in the production of assessable income. The cost of dredging and the cost of navigational aids were accordingly not deductible under s. 88.

Allders International Pty Ltd v Commissioner of State Revenue in his capacity as Comptroller of Stamps Commonwealth Constitution - Exclusive legislative power - With respect to a Commonwealth place - Characterisation of State law - Whether State stamp duty payable on a lease of part of a Commonwealth place. Taxation - State stamp duty - Nature of stamp duty - Whether payable on a lease of part of a Commonwealth place. BRENNAN CJ. Tullamarine Airport was constructed on land acquired for the purpose by the Commonwealth of Australia. The Commonwealth remains registered as the proprietor of an estate in fee simple in that land. The Federal Airports Corporation Act 1986 (Cth) ("the FAC Act ") established the Federal Airports Corporation ("FAC") as a body corporate in which, pursuant to s 28(1) of that Act, Tullamarine Airport [1] was vested "without any conveyance, transfer or assignment". The FAC holds Tullamarine Airport "for and on behalf of the Commonwealth" [2] . It is a "place acquired by the Commonwealth" for a public purpose within the meaning of those words in s 52(i) of the Constitution . In exercise of its statutory powers [3] , the FAC granted a lease to the appellant ("Allders") of a shop at the Tullamarine Airport to conduct the business of a duty free and sales tax free concession. The instrument of lease demised the premises for a term certain expiring on 31 October 2000 [4] . The rent reserved was a fixed sum of $12 per annum (if demanded) plus a variable component calculated according to formulae the factors of which included the number of inbound and outbound international passengers and the average levels of their expenditure on goods to be sold by the lessee [5] . The instrument of lease was executed in New South Wales. Pursuant to s 32 of the Stamps Act 1958 (Vic) ("the Act"), Allders required the Commissioner of State Revenue in his capacity as Comptroller of Stamps of Victoria to express an opinion as to whether the instrument of lease was chargeable with duty and, if so, with what amount. In order to obtain that opinion, the solicitors for Allders lodged the executed lease with the Commissioner. The Commissioner expressed the opinion that the instrument of lease was dutiable and that duty should be assessed ad valorem on the rent calculated and paid in accordance with s 83A of the Act. Section 83A applies to a lease for a definite term of not less than 12 months where the rent cannot be ascertained at the time of execution of the lease. The calculation is based on an estimate and is re-calculated on annual re-estimates of the rent during the term of the lease. Stamp duty is chargeable on instruments pursuant to s 17(1) of the Act which reads as follows: " Subject to the exemptions contained in the Third Schedule and in any Acts for the time being in force, there shall be charged for the use of Her Majesty upon the several instruments specified in the said Schedule the several duties and additional duties therein specified." Social Security - age pension - whether "a de facto spouse" Social Security Act 1947 s.6, 28 (1A) (a) Lynham v Director-General of Social Security 52 ALR 128 Wilson v Secretary to the Department of Social Security 6 August 1985. HEARING CANBERRA 31:10:1985 ORDER The Tribunal sets aside the decision under review and remits the matter to the respondent with a direction that the applicant be granted an age pension pursuant to s.28 (1A) (a) of the Social Security Act 1947 as from the date of his application, being 24 October 1984. Liberty to apply is reserved. DECISION The applicant is 80 years of age. He is the tenant of a State Housing Department unit at Chigwell which he shares with a Mrs. Nankivell who is 75. Both receive an age pension but since July 1971 the respondent has treated them as if they were legally married to each other. In order to test the situation the applicant lodged a fresh application for a full pension on 24 October 1984. It was rejected and following appeal to the Social Security Appeals Tribunal that rejection was confirmed on 1 May 1985. The applicant now seeks review of the decision to reject his claim. It being common ground that the applicant and Mrs. Nankivell have lived together on a bona fide domestic basis at all relevant times the only question for decision is whether he is living with her as her husband. Administrative Law - Judicial review - Decision made under an enactment - Validity of enactment under challenge in High Court in separate proceedings by third parties - Decision attacked on grounds that decision-maker failed to take into account possible invalidity of enactment - Decision also attacked on grounds that enactment invalid - Whether a decision "under an enactment" - Whether decision open to review - Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth), ss 3 (1), 5 (1). The Taxation (Unpaid Company Tax) Assessment Act 1982 (Cth) (TUCTA Act) incorporates, by reference, many of the provisions of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth) (ITA Act). Relying on s. 264 of the ITA Act, as incorporated into the TUCTA Act, the Commissioner issued a notice to the applicants requesting information about the sale of certain shares and seeking production of certain documents. At the time, the constitutional validity of the TUCTA Act had been challenged in the High Court in separate proceedings by third parties. The High Court had reserved its decision. The applicants sought an extension of time to comply with the notice until such time as the High Court delivered its decision. The Commissioner refused. Proceedings were commenced by the applicant under the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth) Judicial Review Act for review of the Commissioner's decision to refuse the extension. The applicant claimed, inter alia, that the Commissioner ought to have taken certain matters into account, all of which were based on the possibility of the High Court holding that the TUCTA Act was invalid. The applicant also sought to argue that the TUCTA Act was in fact invalid and that the Commissioner's decision to issue the notice was therefore invalid. The Commissioner claimed, inter alia, that the decisions sought to be reviewed were excluded by Sched. 1, par. (e) of the Judicial Review Act, that he had no power to extend the time in any event, and that the applicants could not assert the invalidity of an enactment as a ground for review of a decision purportedly made under it. Held: (1) The Commissioner has ample power and discretion under s. 8 of the ITA Act (which provides for the Commissioner to have the general administration of the Act) to extend the time previously fixed by him for compliance with a notice under s. 264. Both sections are incorporated, by reference, into the TUCTA Act. (2) The decisions to serve the notices and the decisions to refuse the applicant's request for an extension of time for compliance are not decisions making, or forming part of the process of making, or leading up to the making of assessments of tax. Therefore par. (e) of Sched. 1 to the Judicial Review Act does not exclude the decisions from review under that Act. Tooheys Ltd v. Minister for Business and Consumer Affairs [1982] FCA 128 ; (1982) 42 ALR 260 , referred to. (3) A decision made under what purports to have been an Act of the Commonwealth Parliament is a decision "under an enactment" for the purposes of the Judicial Review Act, and it is therefore open to review notwithstanding that the only attack upon the decision is an attack upon the validity of the legislation under which it was made. This follows from the wide construction that should be given to the intended operation of the Judicial Review Act. Collector of Customs (N.S.W.) v. Brian Lawlor Automotive Pty Ltd [1979] FCA 21 ; (1979) 41 FLR 338 , per Bowen C.J. at 341-344; Sean Investments Pty Ltd v. Mackellar [1981] FCA 191 ; (1981) 38 ALR 363 , per Deane J. at 370-371; and Lamb v. Moss [1983] FCA 254 ; (1983) 49 ALR 533 , referred to. (4) The matters (flowing from the possible invalidity of the TUCTA Act), claimed by the applicant to have been relevant considerations which, it was said, the Commissioner failed to take into account in refusing an extension are certainly matters which he could have taken into account if he had chosen to do so. However, it has not been shown that he was bound, in the circumstances, to take them into account. The Commissioner's discretions to issue a notice under s. 264 and to extend the time for compliance with it are completely unfettered and it is a matter for him how he exercises them. R. v. ABC; Ex parte 2HD Pty Ltd [1979] HCA 62 ; (1979) 144 CLR 45 at 49-50; and Sean Investments Pty Ltd v. Mackellar [1981] FCA 191 ; (1981) 38 ALR 363 , per Deane J. at 374-375, applied. Ahern v. Deputy Commissioner of Taxation [1983] FCA 279 ; (1983) 14 ATR 807 , distinguished. (5) Because a decision of the High Court, to be handed down in the near future, will resolve the question of the validity of the TUCTA Act, it would be futile for this Court to hear argument on that question directed to showing that the decision to issue the notice was invalid.
